extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy; general educated public interested in pragmatism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging when a belief or theory counts as true from a pragmatist perspective; contrasts these with rationalist definitions of truth. Focuses on verification, usefulness, coherence, and provisionality of beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as instruments of action
rubrics_metrics.description: The possession of true thoughts means everywhere the possession of invaluable instruments of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True beliefs are valuable because they serve as tools for action; truth is tied to practical consequences and the capacity of ideas to guide effective behavior. Example: thinking a cow-path leads to a human habitation can save a starving person lost in woods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as a 'leading that is worthwhile' (verification-process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primarily, and on the common-sense level, the truth of a state of mind means this function of A LEADING THAT IS WORTH WHILE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A true idea is one that starts a verification-process by guiding us into particulars of experience and producing advantageous connections. The central test of truth is whether the idea leads to future experiences that are worth having (i.e., verifiable and beneficial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical value derived from importance of object
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical value of true ideas is primarily derived from the practical importance of their objects to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An idea's usefulness (and hence its truth-status in pragmatist terms) depends on whether its object matters in our life. Some truths may be latent until their objects become relevant; storing general truths for possible future emergencies is prudent.

rubrics_metrics.name: True = starts verification; useful = completed function in experience
rubrics_metrics.description: You can say of it either that 'it is useful because it is true' or that 'it is true because it is useful.' Both phrases mean exactly the same thing, namely that here is an idea that gets fulfilled and can be verified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equivalence links the concept of truth with the process and outcome of verification: 'true' names the idea that initiates verification, while 'useful' names the idea's function when verification has been realized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct verification as prototype of truth-process
rubrics_metrics.description: Such simply and fully verified leadings are certainly the originals and prototypes of the truth-process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct, face-to-face verifications (e.g., following an imagined cow-path and finding a house) are the paradigmatic instances of truth. Other truth-processes are intelligible as modifications, arrests, or substitutions of these primary verifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect or circumstantial verification counts as truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect as well as direct verifications pass muster. Where circumstantial evidence is sufficient, we can go without eye-witnessing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beliefs supported by coherent circumstantial evidence (e.g., assuming a clock from its face without seeing the works; assuming Japan exists) are pragmatically true so long as they 'work'—i.e., lead to no frustration or contradiction in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid waywardness: beliefs must respect experiential regularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth, in these cases, meaning nothing but eventual verification, is manifestly incompatible with waywardness on our part. Woe to him whose beliefs play fast and loose with the order which realities follow in his experience: they will lead him nowhere or else make false connexions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: beliefs that ignore or contradict the regular sequences and connexions in experience are unreliable and will not function as true guides. Reliability and conformity to experiential order are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement = guidance to reality or its surroundings (practical/intellectual handling)
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'agree' in the widest sense with a reality, can only mean to be guided either straight up to it or into its surroundings, or to be put into such working touch with it as to handle either it or something connected with it better than if we disagreed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreement with reality is defined in terms of functional guidance: an idea 'agrees' if it leads us to or enables better handling of the real thing (intellectually or practically); copying is one way but not the essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names and concepts true if they set up verification-processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Names are just as 'true' or 'false' as definite mental pictures are. They set up similar verification-processes, and lead to fully equivalent practical results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linguistic or symbolic representations count as true when they reliably lead to the same verifications and practical results as concrete mental images do. Consistent use of names is required to preserve connections with other truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth relies on communal/coherent verification (credit system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth lives, in fact, for the most part on a credit system. Our thoughts and beliefs 'pass,' so long as nothing challenges them, just as bank-notes pass so long as nobody refuses them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many beliefs are accepted because of others' verifications and the mutual trading of verifications in society; such social/coherent backing is part of what sustains truth in practical life, but ultimately points back to concrete verifications somewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization across kinds: verified on one specimen, applied to others
rubrics_metrics.description: When we have once directly verified our ideas about one specimen of a kind, we consider ourselves free to apply them to other specimens without verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pragmatic truth permits and depends on successful generalization by kinds; a mind that discerns kinds and acts by their laws without pausing to verify will be 'true' in most emergencies. This justifies inductive application of truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirectly or potentially verifying processes are as true as full verifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirectly or only potentially verifying processes may thus be true as well as full verification-processes. They work as true processes would work, give us the same advantages, and claim our recognition for the same reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count as true any process that functions practically like a fully verified process, even if the direct verification is not presently performed; their legitimacy comes from producing equivalent advantages and leading toward verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theories must 'work': mediate between previous truths and new experience
rubrics_metrics.description: We must find a theory that will WORK; and that means something extremely difficult; for our theory must mediate between all previous truths and certain new experiences. It must derange common sense and previous belief as little as possible, and it must lead to some sensible terminus or other that can be verified exactly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for choosing scientific or theoretical accounts: maximal compatibility with existing verified truths, minimal unnecessary disturbance to prior belief, and provision of a verifiable terminus. The obligation to 'work' constrains hypotheses tightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: When empirically equivalent, prefer elegance/economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes alternative theoretic formulas are equally compatible with all the truths we know, and then we choose between them for subjective reasons... 'poor scientific taste' to choose the more complicated of two equally well-evidenced conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie-breaker rule: when empirical adequacy is equal, choose the simpler, more elegant, or more economical theory (principle of parsimony/Occam-like preference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as a made, habitual, and functional property (mutable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is MADE, just as health, wealth and strength are made, in the course of experience. 'The true,' to put it very briefly, is only the expedient in the way of our thinking... The 'absolutely' true... is that ideal vanishing-point towards which we imagine that all our temporary truths will some day converge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pragmatist view: truth is a product of ongoing experiential processes and habits; truths are provisional and subject to revision as experience 'boils over.' The absolute truth is an ideal goal, not an immediately given property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to acknowledge truth is conditional on expediency
rubrics_metrics.description: The obligation to acknowledge truth is grounded in practical expediencies; concrete truths need be recognized only when their recognition is expedient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral/epistemic duty to state or act on truths is context-sensitive: if a true statement is irrelevant to the situation, its expression isn't obligatory. Example: telling someone's address when asked the time is true but not obligatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationalist alternatives: truth as unconditional claim or imperative duty (criticized)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two rationalist definitions offered: (1) 'Truth is just the system of propositions which have an un-conditional claim to be recognized as valid.' (2) Truth is a name for all those judgments which we find ourselves under obligation to make by a kind of imperative duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rationalist standards are presented and then critiqued as vague or trivial unless handled pragmatically; they are included as contrasting evaluative standards (i.e., truth as an eternal, antecedent relation rather than a pragmatic, process-based quality).
